Naive Bayes goes back to a line of probabilistic thinking that begins with Thomas Bayes, whose work on inverse probability led to Bayes’ rule: how to update a belief when new evidence appears. The Naive Bayes classifier turns this rule into a practical method by assuming that the features of an example are independent of each other once the class is known. The assumption is rarely true, but it makes the model fast to train, easy to interpret, and robust when data is sparse. Text collections are the classic case: they are high-dimensional and dominated by rare terms, and Naive Bayes breaks the evidence into one small contribution per term. Learning reduces to counting how often terms occur in the documents of each class, which scales to large collections and updates easily when new documents arrive. For these reasons, Naive Bayes remains a standard baseline, and it performs well when only a few labeled examples per class exist.

A text classifier with a large vocabulary adds a lot of noise: most terms say nothing about the class.

keeps only the terms whose presence or absence is correlated with the class. For each term and class, a four-field table counts the documents with and without the term, inside and outside the class. A strong correlation in any field marks the term as discriminative. The chi-square test and the mutual information, introduced in
, are the most common measures; a simpler alternative selects the terms with the highest weight, as in the term weighting of classical text retrieval.

The independence assumption is wrong for almost every real dataset: “machine” and “learning” occur together far more often than chance predicts. Naive Bayes therefore double-counts correlated evidence, and its probabilities are usually too extreme, close to 0 or 1. Its decisions are nevertheless often right, because classification only needs the correct class to have the highest score, not a correct probability. When calibrated probabilities matter, for example to choose a decision threshold as in
, the scores need to be recalibrated on validation data. Discriminative models such as the logistic regression of
Linear Classifiers: Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines
learn the decision boundary directly and avoid the independence assumption, at the cost of needing more training data.
